## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. The preimage of an algebraic set under $f$ is an algebraic set. In fact, this holds for *any* morphism $\mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbb{C}} \to \mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbb{C}}$; the hypotheses of surjectivity and finite fibers are not needed for this conclusion.

---

### Setup

A morphism $f : \mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbb{C}} \to \mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbb{C}}$ is given by $n+1$ homogeneous polynomials $F_0, \ldots, F_n \in \mathbb{C}[X_0, \ldots, X_n]$ of the same degree $d$, with no common zero on $\mathbb{P}^n$ (i.e., $\gcd(F_0,\ldots,F_n)=1$ as homogeneous polynomials, or equivalently $V(F_0,\ldots,F_n) = \varnothing$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$). Concretely, $f([X_0:\cdots:X_n]) = [F_0(X):\cdots:F_n(X)]$.

### Algebraic argument

Let $Y \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ be an algebraic set. Then $Y = V(g_1, \ldots, g_m)$ for some homogeneous polynomials $g_1, \ldots, g_m \in \mathbb{C}[Y_0, \ldots, Y_n]$.

A point $p = [X_0:\cdots:X_n] \in \mathbb{P}^n$ lies in $f^{-1}(Y)$ if and only if $f(p) \in Y$, i.e.,

$$g_i\big(F_0(X), \ldots, F_n(X)\big) = 0 \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \ldots, m.$$

Define $h_i(X_0,\ldots,X_n) := g_i(F_0(X), \ldots, F_n(X))$. Since each $g_i$ is homogeneous (say of degree $e_i$) and each $F_j$ is homogeneous of degree $d$, each $h_i$ is homogeneous of degree $e_i \cdot d$. Therefore:

$$f^{-1}(Y) = V(h_1, \ldots, h_m) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n,$$

the common zero locus of homogeneous polynomials, which is an algebraic set. $\square$

### Topological argument (alternative)

A morphism of varieties is continuous with respect to the Zariski topology. Algebraic sets in $\mathbb{P}^n$ are precisely the Zariski-closed subsets. The preimage of a closed set under a continuous map is closed. Hence $f^{-1}(Y)$ is Zariski-closed, i.e., algebraic.

### Remark on the hypotheses

The conditions that $f$ is surjective and has finite fibers imply (since $\mathbb{P}^n$ is proper, so a quasi-finite morphism from a proper variety is finite) that $f$ is a **finite morphism**. Finite morphisms are closed, so under these additional hypotheses $f$ also maps algebraic sets *forward* to algebraic sets (i.e., $f$ is a closed map). But for the *preimage* direction asked in the problem, continuity alone suffices, and the surjectivity/finiteness conditions play no role.

### PROOF COMPLETE
